newsitem.title: FRANCE: French bakers savour victory over supermarkets.
newsitem.headline: French bakers savour victory over supermarkets.

text.p: Bakers are savouring a victory over supermarkets under a new law protecting their baguettes from cut-price rivals in a campaign to revive fading French appetite for bread.

Up to 5,000 shops selling bread in France will have to take down "Bakery" signs under the laws in force from New Year's Day, the latest in a long series to safeguard artisans and village corner shops from the ravages of competition.

The laws state that bakers must select their flour, knead dough and bake bread on their premises. Supermarkets and shops which merely heat up factory-made frozen dough will have to use less attractive signs such as "bread stop".
And shops will no longer be able to sell bread below cost to lure in customers to buy other goods.

"The law is a big step forward," said Jocelyne Rolin at the Montmartre bakery in central Paris, which sells about 800 baguettes a day. "People will know what they're buying. It will make it harder to fool people into buying bread taken from a freezer."
"If the law's properly enforced, it will make a difference and could help protect bakery jobs," said Genevieve Lelan at her nearby bakery. "But people have fallen into bad habits."
Bakers work gruelling hours -- Rene Collier, whose bakery employs 14 people in Paris, works from 3 a.m. to midday, sleeps part of the afternoon and then works from 4 p.m. to 7 p.m.
In his bakery, baguette mix rolls out of a machine looking like white snakes before going into the oven for 20 minutes to reappear crispy and golden on the outside and moist inside.

The French daily Le Monde hailed the reform as a "small revolution" for bakers, whose stick-like baguette is an icon of French culture and was long a staple food, like potatoes were in Ireland or rice was in Japan.

But consumption has slumped from the days when Queen Marie-Antoinette could fuel the 1789 Revolution with her reputed remark "Let them eat cake" when told the poor were starving for lack of bread. She was beheaded with her husband Louis XVI.
The French millers' association has said that French people's bread consumption had fallen to about 125 grams (four oz) a day from almost a kilo (2.2 pounds) at the start of the century.
In the past 30 years, the number of bakeries has fallen by about 20,000 to 35,000. The new laws will also oblige new bakers to have a diploma in bread-making.
Jean Pierre Raffarin, minister of Small and Medium Business, Commerce and Craft, said officials had begun making rounds before the New Year and warned about 30 "false bakeries" to take down signs.
"In the end between 3,000 and 5,000 bakeries will have to change their name in the coming weeks," he told Le Parisien daily.
The new laws also outlaw selling bread at a loss -- sometimes baguettes can be bought for just 1.5 francs (29 cents) in a supermarket against about four francs (77 cents) in a bakery.
